topics.title: MCP Goes Stateless: What the 2026-07-28 Spec Breaks in Your MCP Server
topics.whyTrending: Final spec shipped July 28, 2026 (6 days ago). Kills the initialize/initialized handshake and session IDs, adds Multi Round-Trip Requests, header-based routing (Mcp-Method/Mcp-Name), cacheable lists with ttlMs/cacheScope, RFC 9207 issuer validation. Roots, Sampling and Logging deprecated with a 12-month runway; HTTP+SSE transport sunsetting. Every MCP server author has to migrate and nobody has written the practical guide yet.

topics.title: Next.js 16.3: Instant Navigations and the 90% Dev Memory Drop, Benchmarked
topics.whyTrending: Released August 3, 2026 — literally yesterday. Up to 90% less memory in dev, faster builds and rendering, plus 'Instant Navigations': a suite that brings SPA responsiveness back to the App Router. Turbopack persistent build cache and the Rust React Compiler landed in the same train. Zero coverage on the blog and huge search intent right after a release.

topics.title: Next.js Is Now an Agent-First Framework: AGENTS.md, First-Party Skills and Agent Browser
topics.whyTrending: Next.js 16.3 ships bundled docs through AGENTS.md, first-party Skills, and an Agent Browser with React introspection — the framework is explicitly designing for coding agents as a user class. Pairs perfectly with the blog's existing agentic-engineering line and nobody has written the hands-on 'wire your agent into Next.js' guide.

topics.title: Chrome DevTools for Agents 1.0: Stop Letting Your Coding Agent Program Blindfolded
topics.whyTrending: Chrome DevTools for agents hit 1.0 — official MCP server plus agentic skills that give Claude Code, Cursor and Gemini real performance traces, network requests and console errors from a live browser. Turns 'generate and hope' into 'observe, analyze, fix'. Natural follow-up to the WebMCP post, and a comparison against Vercel's agent-browser is a genuinely open question.

topics.title: TypeScript 7.0 One Month In: The Migration Blockers Nobody Warned You About
topics.whyTrending: TS 7.0 went stable July 8, 2026 with 8-12x faster builds — but the missing programmatic API means Vue, Svelte, Astro and MDX users can't get full editor support until 7.1 (~October). The blog's April Project Corsa post was pre-GA; this is the honest post-GA readiness check with real upgrade data, and search volume for 'typescript 7 migration' is peaking now.

topics.title: Terminal-Bench 2.1: Why the Coding Agent Leaderboard Lies to You
topics.whyTrending: GPT-5.6 Sol leads at 89.5% with Opus 5 at 89.1% — a 0.4pt gap that gets reported as a winner. But Opus 5's run used Opus 4.8 as a refusal fallback: count those nine tasks as failures and 84.64% becomes 81.27%. Strong contrarian angle on benchmark methodology at a moment when everyone is picking models off leaderboards.

topics.title: Vercel's New Security Release Program: 9 CVEs and What Next.js LTS Actually Means Now
topics.whyTrending: The July 20, 2026 release fixed 4 HIGH and 5 MEDIUM severity issues, and Vercel formalized a security release process with Active LTS (16.2.11) and Maintenance LTS (15.5.21). Version-pinning strategy for Next.js just changed. Ties directly into the blog's existing Vercel breach and supply-chain posts.

topics.title: fallbackModel and Safe Mode: Making Claude Code Sessions Survive 529s
topics.whyTrending: Chained fallback models (up to three, tried in order on overload) plus Safe Mode are GA, and 529 overload errors are the single most common complaint in long agent runs. Concrete config-file guide with a 3-tier failover setup — practical, code-heavy, and directly useful to the blog's Claude Code audience.

topics.title: Ship Your Own Claude Code Plugin: Marketplace, Validation and Distribution
topics.whyTrending: The community tool marketplace is GA and the August 4, 2026 release added plugin-validation warnings for names Claude Desktop's managed sync would reject. There's an early-mover window for a real end-to-end 'build, validate, publish' guide — the blog already covers skills, hooks and subagents, so this closes the loop.

topics.title: Test-Driven Agentic Development: The Only Agent Workflow That Survives Production
topics.whyTrending: Consensus emerging across dev.to and HN that TDD is what makes agentic coding actually work: you write or co-write the tests, confirm they capture the right behavior, and let the agent iterate against them. Karpathy's 'agentic engineering' framing has taken hold and teams are restructuring around it. Natural sequel to the vibe-coding-to-agentic-engineering post.
